scenes.intro: Timothy and Melanie, welcome. Here is your plan, drawn as your own home. Your score is 60 out of 100, a stable place to build from. Let us look at each part together.
scenes.pillar_savings_and_cash_flow: Your plumbing is savings and monthly cash flow, and it is solid: 26 out of 30 points. You both earn employer matches and retirement saving is on track. The weak spot is spending: the figure is uncertain, and college saving would take about $4,609.22 a year more. In daily life you have breathing room, but little margin for surprise.
scenes.pillar_debt: Your walls are debt, and they are cracked: 12 out of 20 points. Most of your borrowing is calm and low cost. One wall is not: the $18,000 card at 18%, which is the part of your debt worth understanding. Left alone, that crack keeps costing you while your other loans quietly shrink.
scenes.pillar_investments: Your garden is investments, and it is cracked: 8 out of 15 points. Most of your wealth sits in your home, 44.4% of everything you own, which is not the part that grows. You hold $150,000 in cash against $210,000 invested. In daily life that feels safe, yet it works against you over long years.
scenes.pillar_liquidity_and_emergency_fund: Your foundations are your emergency fund and the cash you can reach quickly, and they are solid: 15 out of 15 points. You hold $150,801 in cash, about 16 months of essentials, well past the 8 to 9 months recommended. Even after a $6,000 vacation payment, roughly 15.4 months remain. That cushion is what stands between you and a bad month.
scenes.pillar_insurance_and_protection: Your roof is insurance and protection, and it is broken: 7 out of 20 points. Timothy's life cover sits $610,000 short of the recommended minimum, and Melanie's falls short too. You have no umbrella cover, the extra layer that stands behind your home. If either of you were gone, the mortgage and the children's costs would still be there.
scenes.person_timothy: Timothy, this is your part of the home. You earn $150,000 a year, with $70,000 in your work retirement account. Your life cover of $140,000 leaves $610,000 uncovered against the recommended minimum. The card, the mortgage and the car loan sit in your name, so those payments would fall to Melanie and the children if you were gone.
scenes.person_melanie: Melanie, this is your part of the home. You earn $120,000 a year, and the $150,000 cash account and the $55,000 in your work retirement plan are in your name. Your life cover of $110,000 falls $490,000 short of the recommended minimum. For Liam and Josh, that gap would land on top of losing you.
scenes.move_1: One step in your plan is to pay $6,800 on the 18% card from cash you already hold. That repairs your walls, the debt part of the home. It lifts your score from 60 out of 100 to 62 out of 100.
scenes.move_2: Another step is to add $235,000 of life cover, which repairs your roof, the protection over your family. On its own it leaves your score at 60 out of 100. It closes part of the gap between what you have and what the plan says you need.
scenes.move_3: Another step is to add $1M of umbrella cover, the protection that sits behind your home and cars if someone is hurt. That also repairs your roof. On its own it leaves your score at 60 out of 100.
scenes.all_moves: Done together, these steps take your score from 60 out of 100 to 78 out of 100. You pay down the card from cash you already hold, add life cover, and add umbrella cover. Your walls and your roof are the parts that change.
scenes.timeline: Now look ahead. Timothy plans to retire at 62 and Melanie at 60, and the plan has your debts paid off by 2059. Retirement income is projected to cover 93% of what you need each year, and $2,371,901 is projected to remain at the end of the plan. That is your garden still growing for the years after work.
